modules.body:
Welcome to the movement, not just a course

You are joining a program that has trained over 500 professionals across six countries — Cameroon, France, Spain, India, the USA, and Canada — with complete beginners learning beside working engineers. AI Unlocked was born from a simple conviction: the gap between those who can direct AI and those who cannot is becoming the defining inequality of this decade, and no one should be left on the wrong side of it because of geography or budget. This is the antidote to what we call "AI poverty."

"The future is already here — it's just not evenly distributed." — William Gibson. Team21 exists to distribute it. By the end of these four weeks, the future will be in your hands, literally, on the device you're reading this on.

What actually happens over four weeks

This is not a lecture series you passively consume. It is a build program with a rhythm:

  • Week 1 — Foundations & fluency: how AI works, the vocabulary, and the single most valuable skill in the course — prompt engineering with the CLEAR framework.
  • Week 2 — Application & creation: the full tools landscape, multi-modal work, media production, and authoring — you will publish real artifacts.
  • Week 3 — Enterprise & the group project: AI for business (Business Model Canvas, SOSTAC), agentic AI, and a team build presented to the cohort.
  • Week 4 — Capstone & graduation: a real, working project of your own — past cohorts have shipped published books, working apps, new businesses, and digital-marketing agencies.

The plAIbox™ culture

Throughout the course you will meet plAIbox™ labs — graded, scenario-based challenges where you build something real using AI: an organization, a media campaign, a business plan, a book. You share outputs with your cohort and your mentor. The house rule is printed on every lab: Be CreAItive — work smarter, not harder. The labs are where learning becomes ability. You cannot pass this course by reading; you pass it by building.

Mentorship: you are never alone

Every learner has a human mentor. This is what separates Team21 from a YouTube playlist. Your mentor reviews your labs, answers what confuses you, and holds you to the standard. Your first action this week: open the My Mentor tab and book your kickoff call.

Before we begin: capture your starting point

Answer these four questions in your learning journal. You will revisit them at graduation, and the contrast will surprise you:

  • What is your background, and what do you do today?
  • What do you honestly know about AI right now?
  • What would you most love to accomplish with AI — a project, a business, a skill?
  • Before we talk about AI — how do you think we got here technologically?
The Team21 AI Commandments — these govern everything we do and never change:
1. Investigate — understand — apply. Never use a tool you don't understand on work that matters.
2. Review for hallucinations. Always keep a human in the loop; AI drafts, you decide.
3. Do no harm. Your skills are power; use them to build up, never to deceive or exploit.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Keep a prompt journal from day one. Every prompt that works is an asset you'll reuse for years — the Prompt Library tab is your starter kit.
  • Publish before you're ready. The learners who finish are the ones who share messy first drafts, not the ones waiting for perfection.
  • Teach as you learn. Explaining a concept to a friend (or to the AI) is the fastest way to master it.

📚 Glossary

  • plAIbox™: a Team21 graded, hands-on lab where you build a real artifact with AI.
  • Mentor: the human coach assigned to review your work and guide your progress.
  • Capstone: your final Week-4 project that proves your capability.
  • Hallucination: when AI states false information confidently (Module 4 goes deep).

modules.t: From Web 1.0 to the AI Era
modules.d: How we got here — read-only, read-write, read-write-own — and what intelligence really means.
modules.body:
To understand where AI is taking us, understand where the web has been

Artificial intelligence did not arrive from nowhere. It is the culmination of three decades of the internet evolving from something you read, to something you write, to something that increasingly thinks alongside you. Seeing this arc turns AI from a mysterious disruption into the logical next chapter — and helps you predict what comes next.

Web 1.0 — the "Read-Only" web (1990s–early 2000s)

The first web was a library, not a conversation. A small number of technical people created static HTML pages; everyone else simply looked. Think GeoCities, early Yahoo, AOL, Netscape, guest books. You could consume information, but you could not easily participate. Publishing required knowing code and owning a server. The web was a broadcast medium wearing a browser's clothes.

Web 2.0 — the "Read-Write" web (2004–2020)

Then the web learned to listen. Blogs (WordPress), wikis (Wikipedia), and social platforms (Facebook, YouTube, Twitter) turned every user into a potential publisher. Cloud computing (Google Drive, Dropbox) and SaaS tools (Slack, Trello) meant software lived in the browser, updated constantly, and connected everyone. Mobile put it all in your pocket. The defining shift: value moved from those who owned the presses to those who created the content. Billions of people became creators.

Web 3.0 — the "Read-Write-Own" era (2020–present)

The current chapter adds ownership and intelligence: decentralization, digital identity, and blockchain give users a stake — but the transformation everyone actually feels is AI integration. Intelligence itself became a utility you can summon on demand, like electricity from a socket. The web no longer just stores and connects human knowledge; it actively generates, reasons over, and acts on it. That is the era you are learning to operate in.

Each web era moved value to a new group: Web 1.0 rewarded publishers, Web 2.0 rewarded creators, and Web 3.0 rewards those who can direct intelligence. This course is your qualification for the third group.

So what actually IS artificial intelligence?

Stripped of hype: AI is the effort to give machines intelligence — the ability to perform tasks that normally require human minds. And intelligence, whether in a person or a program, is a loop of four abilities:

  • Perceive: gather information from the environment (text, images, sound, sensor data).
  • Analyze: process and make sense of what was gathered.
  • Determine a response: decide what to do based on that analysis.
  • Act appropriately: take suitable action — and observe the result to improve.
Field lesson (from our Yaoundé classroom): walk through a busy open-air market like marché Mokolo and your brain runs this loop hundreds of times a minute — perceiving a gap in the crowd, analyzing a vendor's price, deciding to haggle, acting, and adjusting. Every AI system is an attempt to imitate that same perceive–analyze–decide–act cycle, powered by data instead of neurons.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Predict the next era. If Web 3.0 is "read-write-own + intelligence," ask yourself what "act autonomously" (agentic AI) will change — you'll study exactly that in Week 3.
  • Use the loop as a design tool. When building anything with AI, check: does it perceive good data? analyze well? decide with a human? act safely?

📚 Glossary

  • Web 1.0 / 2.0 / 3.0: read-only / read-write / read-write-own eras of the internet.
  • SaaS: Software as a Service — software you use in the browser by subscription.
  • Decentralization: distributing control away from a single authority (a Web 3.0 theme).
  • Intelligence (operational): the perceive → analyze → decide → act loop.

📖 Explore further

  • Stanford HAI — AI Index Report, for how fast this era is moving.
  • Tim Berners-Lee on the web's evolution — webfoundation.org.

modules.d: Data types, how machines learn, and the iron law of Garbage In → Garbage Out.
modules.body:
Everything AI does, it does with data

If intelligence is the engine, data is the fuel. An AI system is only ever as good as what it learned from. This is not a technicality — it is the single most important thing a non-technical professional can understand about AI, because it explains both the miracles and the failures you'll encounter.

The kinds of data AI consumes

  • Text — books, articles, code, conversations (the fuel of ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini).
  • Images — photos, diagrams, scans (fuel for vision and image-generation models).
  • Audio — speech and music (fuel for transcription, voice, and music tools).
  • Video — moving images with sound (the newest frontier).
  • Numeric & sensor — spreadsheets, prices, temperatures, GPS (fuel for prediction).

How machines actually learn: three styles

  • Supervised learning — learning from labeled examples. Show a model thousands of emails tagged "spam" or "not spam," and it learns the pattern. Most practical AI today is supervised.
  • Unsupervised learning — finding hidden structure in unlabeled data. Give it your customers and it discovers segments you never knew existed.
  • Reinforcement learning — learning by trial, reward, and penalty, like training a dog or mastering a game. It's how systems learn to improve through consequences.
"In God we trust. All others must bring data." — attributed to W. Edwards Deming. Modern AI is Deming's aphorism made mechanical: without data, even the cleverest architecture knows nothing.

The iron law: GIGO — Garbage In, Garbage Out

If the data feeding an AI is biased, incomplete, or wrong, the output will be too — delivered with the same fluent confidence as a correct answer. This is why professionals interrogate data before trusting any AI built on it. Whenever you evaluate a dataset — or an AI answer resting on one — ask:

  • Who collected it, and might they have an agenda?
  • Where did it come from, and is that source representative?
  • What quality is it, and what bias might it carry (whose reality is missing)?
The AI Success Formula: Quality Data + Skilled People + Computing Power + Advanced Algorithms = an effective AI system. You are being trained to be the "Skilled People" — the irreplaceable human judgment in that equation.

🧪 Validated exercise

🔬 Going deeper: bias, representativeness and data quality in practice

GIGO has a subtle cousin: biased data. A model trained mostly on one group's records will perform worse for others — for example, a credit model trained on salaried urban workers may misjudge market traders whose income is irregular but reliable. Data can be accurate and still unrepresentative. Before trusting any AI output that affects people, ask: Whose data trained this? Who is missing? How recent is it?

Data quality has four practical dimensions you can check in your own work: accuracy (is it correct?), completeness (are there gaps?), consistency (are formats and definitions the same?), and timeliness (is it current?). When you give AI a spreadsheet to analyse, clean these first — remove duplicates, standardise dates and currencies, fill or flag missing values. The same model produces sharply better insight from clean data.

Finally, data carries responsibility. Personal data — names, phone numbers, health or financial details — must be collected with consent, protected, and shared with AI tools only when their terms allow it. Commandment 3, Do No Harm, applies to data as much as to images and words.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Ask AI for its sources. When an answer matters, ask "what is this based on, and how confident are you?" — you're probing the data behind the fluency.
  • Bias hides in absence. The most dangerous data problem is not what's wrong — it's whose reality was never collected at all.

📚 Glossary

  • Supervised / unsupervised / reinforcement learning: learning from labels / from structure / from reward.
  • GIGO: Garbage In, Garbage Out.
  • Bias (data): systematic skew in data that becomes skew in output.
  • Training data: the examples a model learns from.

📖 Explore further

  • Cathy O'Neil, Weapons of Math Destruction — how biased data harms real people.
  • Google's Machine Learning Crash Course (free).

modules.d: Generative vs predictive, ANI/AGI/ASI, and the terms every professional must know.
modules.body:
Speak the language, command the room

You don't need to be an engineer, but you do need to speak AI fluently enough to make good decisions, ask sharp questions, and not be sold snake oil. This module is your working vocabulary — the terms that appear in every headline, sales pitch, and strategy meeting.

Two great families of AI

  • Generative AI — creates new content: text, images, music, video, code. This is what powers ChatGPT, Claude, Midjourney, Suno. It is the revolution of the last few years.
  • Predictive AI — forecasts outcomes from historical data: sales next quarter, which customer will churn, which transaction is fraud. Older, quieter, and running the world's back offices for years.

The three tiers of AI ambition

  • Narrow AI (ANI, "Weak AI"): superb at ONE kind of task — translation, face recognition, spam filtering, playing chess, or chatting. Every AI that exists today is Narrow AI, including the most impressive chatbots. Powerful, but bounded.
  • General AI (AGI, "Strong AI"): a hypothetical machine that could learn, reason, and adapt across any domain like a human. It does not exist yet, and experts disagree sharply on when — or whether — it will.
  • Superintelligence (ASI): a hypothetical intelligence surpassing the best humans in every field. Entirely theoretical, and the subject of serious safety debate about control and values.
Stuart Russell (Human Compatible) warns that the real risk isn't malevolent robots but highly capable systems pursuing goals we specified carelessly. Knowing the ANI/AGI/ASI ladder lets you tell genuine concern from science-fiction hype.

The terms you'll hear constantly

  • LLM — Large Language Model: an AI trained on vast text (billions of parameters). ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini are LLMs.
  • GPT — Generative Pre-trained Transformer: the architecture behind many LLMs.
  • NLP — Natural Language Processing: AI understanding and producing human language.
  • Multi-modal — handling text, images, audio, and video together in one model.
  • Context window — how much the AI can "hold in mind" at once; bigger windows read whole books.
  • Token — a chunk of text (~¾ of a word) that models process and bill by.
  • Parameter — an internal "dial" a model tunes during training; more (loosely) means more capacity.
  • Hallucination — confidently stated false information. The reason Commandment 2 exists.
  • Fine-tuning — further training a general model on specialized data for a niche.

The honest limits — what today's AI does NOT do well

  • Guarantee accuracy (hallucination is intrinsic, not a bug to be patched away).
  • Know events after its training cutoff, unless connected to live search.
  • Replicate genuine human emotional understanding.
  • Make ethical decisions without human oversight.

🧪 Validated exercise

🔬 Going deeper: how a language model produces an answer

A large language model breaks text into tokens (pieces of words) and predicts the most likely next token, again and again, based on patterns learned during training. It does not look facts up unless connected to search or documents; it generates what is statistically plausible. That is why hallucination is intrinsic: a plausible-sounding but false sentence can be just as "likely" as a true one.

Three practical levers follow. Grounding — giving the model the documents or data to work from (or using tools with search and citations) — sharply reduces invented facts. Context window limits mean very long conversations or documents may exceed what the model can hold at once, so important instructions should be repeated or summarised. Temperature and similar settings, in tools that expose them, trade creativity for consistency: lower settings for factual work, higher for brainstorming.

Understanding this mechanism protects you from both overtrust ("it sounds sure, so it's true") and undertrust ("it's just autocomplete, so it's useless"). It is a powerful pattern engine that needs good inputs and human review.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Spot the hype filter: if someone claims their product is "AGI" or "conscious," you now know that's marketing — all deployed AI is Narrow.
  • Bigger context = new workflows: when a tool boasts a huge context window, that's your cue you can feed it entire documents at once.

📚 Glossary

  • Generative vs Predictive AI: creates content vs forecasts outcomes.
  • ANI / AGI / ASI: narrow (today) / general (hypothetical) / super (theoretical).
  • LLM, GPT, NLP, token, parameter, context window, fine-tuning, hallucination, multi-modal: the working toolkit above.

📖 Explore further

  • Melanie Mitchell, Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans.
  • LMArena leaderboard — lmarena.ai — see today's LLMs ranked.

modules.d: Zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot — and why context is the real superpower.
modules.body:
The highest-leverage skill you will ever learn

Prompt engineering is the craft of instructing AI to get exactly the output you want. It is the difference between a tool that gives generic mush and one that produces professional work. Master this and every other AI skill multiplies. Neglect it and the best model in the world will disappoint you.

"The hottest new programming language is English." — Andrej Karpathy. You already speak the language of the AI age; this module teaches you to speak it precisely.

The three core prompting strategies

  • Zero-shot: give the task with no examples — "Translate this to French." Perfect for simple, common tasks the model already knows cold.
  • One-shot: provide a single example first, then the task. The AI copies your pattern. Use when the format matters more than the model's default.
  • Few-shot: give several examples to firmly lock in a pattern. Best when you need the same structure repeated exactly — product descriptions, report formats, email templates, a house style.
Worked contrast. Zero-shot: "Write a product description for a water bottle." (generic) → Few-shot: paste three of your best existing descriptions, then "Now write one for our new steel bottle in the same voice." (on-brand, instantly usable). Same model, radically different value — the difference is the examples you supplied.

Understand the machine you're driving

  • Context is king. The more relevant background you give, the better the output. "Write an email" is weak; "Write a warm follow-up email to a client who missed our meeting, apologizing for nothing, proposing two new times next week, in my friendly-but-professional voice" is strong. The second prompt did the model's guessing for it.
  • Context windows reset. On free tiers especially, a new session forgets everything — re-supply the essentials each time, or use tools with large windows for long projects.
  • Go multi-modal. Modern AI accepts images ("what's wrong with this design?"), voice (brainstorm out loud), even live conversation. Practice all of them this week.

Practice set — do these today

  • Zero-shot: "Give me 10 low-cost business ideas for my city."
  • Context-rich: paste a real document and ask three precise questions about it.
  • Voice: "Give me 10 ways to spend $100 wisely this month." (spoken)
  • Few-shot: give 2 examples of your writing, then ask for a third in the same voice.
  • Live simulation: "Simulate a panel of two interviewing me for an AI-trainer role; ask one question at a time."
Core principle: AI amplifies your thinking — it doesn't replace it. Lazy prompts scale laziness; sharp prompts scale expertise. The quality of what you get out is governed by the clarity of what you put in.
🧪 Interactive Lab — Match the situation to the strategy

🧪 Try-it lab (copy → run in your AI)

Here are two examples of my writing voice: [paste two short samples]. Study the tone, sentence length, and vocabulary. Now write a third piece on [your topic] in exactly that voice. Before writing, tell me in one line what you noticed about my style.

🔬 Going deeper: chain-of-thought, decomposition and self-critique

Beyond zero-, one- and few-shot prompting, three techniques reliably improve results on harder tasks. Step-by-step reasoning: asking the model to work through a problem in stages ("First list the costs, then calculate totals, then compare") improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning; many modern "reasoning" models do this internally. Decomposition: breaking a big task into a sequence of smaller prompts — outline, then sections, then edit — produces better work than one giant request. Self-critique: after a draft, ask "Review your answer against my requirements; list what is missing or wrong, then improve it." This simple loop catches many errors.

Also learn to constrain: specify what not to do ("no jargon", "under 150 words", "do not invent statistics — mark unknowns as [DATA NEEDED]"). Constraints reduce generic filler and fabrication.

Finally, save what works. Keep a personal prompt library of your best prompts with notes on when to use them. Over weeks, this library becomes one of your most valuable professional assets.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • The magic phrase: end any prompt with "Ask me clarifying questions before you answer" and watch quality jump.
  • Show, don't tell: one good example beats three paragraphs of instructions — that's the whole power of few-shot.

📚 Glossary

  • Zero/One/Few-shot: no examples / one example / several examples in the prompt.
  • Context: the background you supply to frame the task.
  • Multi-modal prompting: using text, image, and voice inputs.

modules.t: Prompt Engineering II: The CLEAR Framework
modules.d: Persona · Tone · Format · Details · Target audience — plus Context, Reference, Iterate, Evaluate.
modules.body:
From lucky prompts to a repeatable system

Module 4 gave you strategies; this gives you a framework so good prompts stop being accidents. The Team21 CLEAR method defines five things in every professional prompt — and four advanced moves that separate operators from dabblers.

The five CLEAR elements

  • Persona — who should the AI BE? "You are an experienced marketing consultant with 10 years in e-commerce…" This single line reshapes everything that follows.
  • Tone — professional, warm, urgent, empathetic, playful. Name it.
  • Format — the exact shape: bullet list, table, memo, 8-slide outline, tweet thread.
  • Details — the specifics and constraints: length, budget, must-includes, must-avoids.
  • Target audience — beginners, executives, teenagers, patients. The same content transforms completely by audience.

The four advanced moves

  • Context — the situation framing the task ("we're launching in a bilingual market and want Gen Z to buy").
  • Reference — a model to emulate or avoid ("with the punch of Nike's 'Just Do It'").
  • Iterate — refine across turns; the first output is a draft, not a verdict.
  • Evaluate — judge the output against your goal and say what to fix.
Real class example — the full stack:
Persona: experienced (10 yrs) digital-business & e-commerce expert. Tone: energetic, useful. Format: weekly teasers for the next month. Details: to sell two wellness products. Audience: Gen Z in a bilingual market. Context: you want Gen Z to live healthier and change their situation. Reference: language with the punch of Nike's "Just Do It."
Every element narrows the output toward something you can actually use.

Industry-grade patterns

  • Healthcare: Persona: Medical Communications Specialist · Tone: empathetic, non-alarmist · Format: patient FAQ · Details: recovery after routine surgery · Audience: elderly patients & caregivers · Reference: WHO health-literacy standards.
  • Data: Persona: Senior Data Scientist · Tone: objective · Format: executive summary with bullets · Details: consumer-spending patterns during inflation · Audience: Board of Directors.
"Always invite AI to the table." — Ethan Mollick, Co-Intelligence. CLEAR is how you make sure it shows up as the right expert, in the right voice, for the right audience — every time.

Reference: [a style to emulate]. Task: [what you want]. Before answering, restate the brief in one line so I can confirm you understood.

🔬 Going deeper: diagnosing a weak prompt with CLEAR

When output disappoints, diagnose which CLEAR element was missing rather than rewriting blindly. Generic voice? Persona or Reference is missing. Wrong length or shape? Format and Details are vague. Too technical or too simple? Target audience is unclear. Feels off in mood? Tone was not named. Misses the point? Context is missing. This diagnostic habit turns prompting from trial-and-error into a skill you can improve deliberately.

Use the advanced moves in sequence. After the first response, Evaluate it against your goal ("This is too formal for teenagers; the second idea is strongest"), then Iterate with specific instructions. Professionals rarely accept a first draft; two or three focused iterations usually produce dramatically better work.

Finally, ask the model to restate the brief before it answers (as in the template). If its summary is wrong, you have caught a misunderstanding before it costs you time — a small habit with large returns.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Save every CLEAR prompt that works into your Prompt Library — you're building a personal asset that compounds.
  • Persona is the biggest lever. Changing only "You are a lawyer" to "You are a plain-language teacher" transforms the entire answer.
  • Iterate out loud: tell the AI "that was too formal and missed the price — redo" and it will. Treat draft one as clay.

📚 Glossary

  • CLEAR: Persona, Tone, Format, Details, Target audience (Team21 framework).
  • Context / Reference / Iterate / Evaluate: the four advanced moves.
  • Persona prompting: assigning the AI an expert identity.

📖 Explore further

  • Team21 Prompt Library (the Prompt Library tab) — dozens of CLEAR prompts ready to adapt.
  • Ethan Mollick, One Useful Thing — practical prompting craft.

Why a serious operator studies the whole board

Most people know two or three AI tools. Operators know the terrain: which model reasons hardest, which is cheapest at scale, which handles a million-token document, which runs on your own hardware for privacy, and which quietly became world-class while everyone looked elsewhere. This module maps the top 20 tools of 2025–26 — including the Chinese frontier (DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen) that reset global price-performance expectations — with honest strengths, real links, and the situations where each is the right call. Prices and limits move monthly; treat figures as teaching snapshots and verify at first use.

"AI is the new electricity." — Andrew Ng. Electricity is a commodity you choose a supplier for; by the end of this module you will choose suppliers deliberately instead of defaulting to the first brand you heard of.

Group A — The frontier generalists (your daily drivers)

  • 1. ChatGPT — OpenAI. The category-definer; deep tool ecosystem (Custom GPTs, voice, image via DALL·E, data analysis, web). Best all-rounder for creativity and breadth. Free tier; Plus ~$20/mo. 🔗 chatgpt.com
  • 2. Claude — Anthropic. Widely preferred for long-form writing, nuanced analysis, coding, and careful reasoning; Projects and large context; strong safety posture. Free tier; Pro ~$20/mo. 🔗 claude.ai
  • 3. Gemini — Google. Massive context window, tight Workspace integration (Docs, Gmail, Sheets), strong multimodal and research. Free tier; Advanced via Google One AI. 🔗 gemini.google.com
  • 4. Microsoft Copilot — the same frontier models woven into Windows and Microsoft 365 (Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams). Best where your work already lives in Office. 🔗 copilot.microsoft.com
  • 5. Grok — xAI. Fast, real-time-leaning, integrated with X; strong on trending topics and image generation; edgier tone. 🔗 grok.com

Group B — The Chinese frontier (the price-performance shock)

Hidden-unlock insight: in late 2024–25 Chinese labs shipped open-weight models that rival Western frontier quality at a fraction of the API cost — a shift that pressured global pricing and made powerful AI dramatically cheaper for builders everywhere. Ignoring them is now an amateur move.
  • 6. DeepSeek — DeepSeek AI. Open-weight models (V3 chat; R1-class reasoning) that stunned the industry by matching top reasoning benchmarks at a small fraction of typical training/serving cost. Free chat; famously cheap API; weights downloadable for self-hosting. Best for: heavy reasoning and coding on a budget, and privacy-sensitive self-hosted deployments. 🔗 deepseek.com
  • 7. Kimi — Moonshot AI. Famous for enormous context (long-document and multi-file analysis) and strong agentic/coding releases; a favorite for ingesting whole books, codebases, or case files. Free chat; API available. Best for: giant-document work and research synthesis. 🔗 kimi.moonshot.cn (intl: kimi.ai)
  • 8. Qwen — Alibaba. A broad open-weight family (text, vision, coding) that consistently ranks near the top of open leaderboards; strong multilingual and Chinese–English work. Free chat; open weights. 🔗 chat.qwen.ai

Group C — Research & knowledge engines

  • 9. Perplexity — answer engine with live web search and inline citations; "Deep Research" mode compiles sourced reports. Best for: cited research and current facts. Free; Pro ~$20/mo. 🔗 perplexity.ai
  • 10. NotebookLM — Google. Grounds answers strictly in YOUR uploaded sources and generates an uncanny two-host "Audio Overview" podcast from them. Best for: study packs, onboarding docs, turning documents into audio. Free. 🔗 notebooklm.google.com

Group D — Media creation (image, video, audio)

  • 11. Midjourney — the aesthetic benchmark for AI imagery; via web + Discord. Subscription from ~$10/mo. 🔗 midjourney.com
  • 12. Ideogram — best-in-class text inside images (posters, logos, signage). Free tier. 🔗 ideogram.ai
  • 13. Canva (Magic Studio) — design for non-designers with AI generation, background removal, and brand kits. Free; Pro tiers. 🔗 canva.com
  • 14. Runway — pioneer of AI video generation and editing (Gen-series). Best for: short-form generative video and effects. Free trial; paid tiers. 🔗 runwayml.com
  • 15. Google Veo / Flow — Google's high-fidelity text-to-video, among the most realistic available; access via Gemini/Flow. 🔗 deepmind.google/models/veo
  • 16. ElevenLabs — the voice standard: lifelike text-to-speech, dubbing, and voice cloning (consent required). Free tier; creator plans. 🔗 elevenlabs.io
  • 17. Suno — full songs (vocals + instruments) from a text prompt; broadcast-ready beds and jingles. Free; Pro tiers. 🔗 suno.com
  • 18. CapCut — fast AI video editing: auto-captions, cuts, effects; the creator's edit bay. Free; Pro. 🔗 capcut.com

Group E — Builder & agent tools

  • 19. Cursor — the AI-native code editor; whole-codebase context and agentic edits. The professional vibe-coder's daily tool. Free tier; Pro ~$20/mo. 🔗 cursor.com
  • 20. Lovable — describe an app in plain English → it builds and deploys a working full-stack web app to a live URL. Best for: non-coders shipping real products fast (pairs with the Vibe Coding course). Free tier; paid plans. 🔗 lovable.dev
Honorable mentions to watch: Google AI Studio (free power-user lab + API), Poe (many models in one place), Hugging Face (open-model hub), Mistral / Le Chat (European frontier, open weights), Meta Llama (open weights powering countless apps), and Manus (agentic task automation). The landscape shifts monthly — a quarterly re-scan is part of staying current.

Choosing well: a decision guide

  • Deep reasoning / analysis / careful writing: Claude, or DeepSeek-R1 for reasoning on a budget.
  • Everyday versatility + ecosystem: ChatGPT.
  • Huge documents / many files at once: Gemini or Kimi (massive context).
  • Cited, current research: Perplexity; grounded in your own docs → NotebookLM.
  • Cheapest capable API / self-hosting for privacy: DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral (open weights).
  • Inside Microsoft/Google workflows: Copilot / Gemini respectively.
  • Media: Midjourney/Ideogram (image), Runway/Veo (video), ElevenLabs (voice), Suno (music), CapCut (edit).
  • Building software: Cursor (code), Lovable (no-code app → live URL).

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Free power tier: Google AI Studio gives system prompts, ~1M-token context, and a free API key — the most underused free tool in AI.
  • Open weights = privacy: DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama and Mistral can run on your own machine/server, so sensitive data never leaves your control.
  • Don't marry one model: route each task to its best tool. Poe or a multi-model workflow lets you compare answers side by side.
  • Reverse-engineer excellence: see output you admire? Ask an AI, "what prompt would produce this?" — then adapt it.
  • Cost math for builders: at scale, the API price gap between frontier Western and open Chinese models can be 10–30× — model choice is a budget decision, not just a quality one.

📰 What just happened in AI (stay current)

  • Chinese open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek R1-class) forced a global re-pricing of AI — top-tier reasoning is now cheap enough to build businesses on.

📖 Glossary

  • Open-weight model: a model whose parameters are downloadable, so anyone can run or fine-tune it on their own hardware (DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral).
  • Context window: how much text a model can consider at once, measured in tokens; larger windows allow whole-book analysis.
  • Token: a chunk of text (~¾ of a word) the model processes; pricing and limits are counted in tokens.
  • Reasoning model: a model tuned to "think" through multi-step problems before answering (e.g. DeepSeek-R1-class, OpenAI o-series).
  • Multimodal: handles more than text — images, audio, video — in one model.
  • API: the programmatic interface developers use to call a model inside their own apps (priced per token).
  • Self-hosting: running an open-weight model on your own server so data never leaves your control.

modules.body:
Your first plAIbox™ — this is where reading becomes ability

You have the foundations and the CLEAR framework. Now you build something real. In this graded lab you will found a complete community nonprofit — mission, name, brand, programs, budget, and launch plan — using AI as your entire founding team. Alumni have turned this exact lab into registered, funded organizations. Take it seriously and it becomes your portfolio's first proof.

The scenario. You have identified a real need in your region — displaced families, out-of-school youth, unemployed graduates, elderly isolation, whatever moves you. You will create the organization that answers it. Use a cause you genuinely care about; passion makes the lab better and the artifact usable.

Part A — Strategy & identity (use your best reasoning AI: Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini)

  1. Mission & vision. Prompt with full CLEAR: "You are a nonprofit strategy consultant. Help me define a mission and vision for an organization addressing [need] in [place]. Ask me 5 questions first, then draft three mission options in different tones."
  2. Name & tagline. Generate 15 candidate names with rationale; shortlist three; test them on a friend.
  3. Theory of change. "Map how our activities lead to outputs, outcomes, and long-term impact as a simple logic chain."
  4. Three core programs. Define them with target beneficiaries and a one-line success measure each.

Part B — Brand & materials

  1. Logo & visual identity: use Ideogram (best for text-in-image) or Canva to generate a logo and pick brand colors.
  2. One-page overview: draft a compelling one-pager for donors — problem, solution, ask.
  3. Social presence: write bios and 5 launch posts for the platforms your community actually uses (in your region, lead with WhatsApp and Facebook).

Part C — Operations & money

  1. Starter budget: "Draft a realistic first-year budget for this organization at small scale, with line items and assumptions I can adjust."
  2. Funding plan: list five realistic funding sources (local grants, diaspora giving, community events, corporate CSR, membership) and a first approach for each.
  3. 90-day launch plan: a week-by-week action list to go from idea to first activity.
Team21 field lesson: in our Yaoundé cohorts this lab often models an organization serving internally displaced families, in line with national NGO law. Keep your build lawful and dignified — Commandment 3, Do No Harm, applies to every beneficiary image and story you generate.

📝 Submission (graded by your mentor)

  • Mission, vision, name, and theory of change.
  • Logo + brand colors + one-page overview.
  • Three programs, first-year budget, funding plan, and 90-day launch plan.
  • Your prompt log: the CLEAR prompts you used, with at least two visible iterations (draft → your critique → better draft). The prompt log is half the grade — it proves the skill, not just the output.
🧪 Kick-off lab (copy → run to begin Part A now)

You are an experienced nonprofit strategy consultant who has founded organizations in resource-limited settings. I want to create a community organization addressing [describe the need] in [your city/region]. Before giving any answer, ask me five sharp questions to understand the community, the beneficiaries, and my own strengths. After I answer, propose three distinct mission statements (different tones), a theory of change as a simple logic chain, and three core programs each with one measurable success indicator.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Route by strength: reasoning & strategy → Claude/ChatGPT; logo & design → Ideogram/Canva; research on real local grants → Perplexity.
  • Make it real: if the cause genuinely matters to you, don't stop at the lab — several alumni actually registered theirs.
  • Dignity check: never generate beneficiary images or stories that demean; represent your community with respect.

📚 Glossary

  • Theory of change: the logic chain from activities → outputs → outcomes → impact.
  • Value/one-pager: a single-page donor overview (problem, solution, ask).
  • CSR: Corporate Social Responsibility — a corporate funding source.

📖 Explore further

  • The full AI Unlocked: NGOs & Nonprofits specialization builds on this lab at professional depth.
  • Canva for Nonprofits — free design for eligible orgs.

modules.body:
AI is no longer just about typing

Modern AI is multi-modal — it sees, hears, speaks, and reasons across formats at once. Learning to use every mode multiplies what you can do, often faster than typing. This module tours the modes and the sector use-cases you'll adapt to your own work.

The four modes, and how to wield each

  • Vision (upload an image): "What's wrong with this design?" · "Redesign this room in teal." · "Extract the table from this photo into a spreadsheet." · "Explain this error screenshot." Point your camera at the world and ask.
  • Voice & live conversation: brainstorm out loud on a walk; run a spoken mock interview; practice a language; have the AI quiz you hands-free. Voice mode changes what's possible while commuting or cooking.
  • Image generation: posters, product mock-ups, illustrations, social graphics (Ideogram, Midjourney, Canva).
  • Video & audio generation: short clips (Runway, Veo), voiceovers (ElevenLabs), music beds (Suno) — studio output from a laptop.
"Always invite AI to the table." — Ethan Mollick. In a multi-modal world, that table has more seats than you think: the AI can be your designer, your interviewer, your translator, and your narrator in a single afternoon.

Use cases we build in class — across industries

  • Marketing & social: a campaign from one idea → copy + images + a short video + a schedule.
  • Education: a lesson turned into slides, a quiz, a leveled reading, and an audio recap.
  • Healthcare (admin side): plain-language patient handouts in two languages (deep-dived in the Medicine specialization).
  • Retail & small business: product photos, descriptions, and a WhatsApp catalog.
  • Real estate: listing descriptions, staged-room visualizations, and buyer FAQs.
  • Agriculture: photo-diagnosis of crop disease, advisory in local language (see the Agriculture specialization).
The through-line: in every sector the pattern is the same — Task → Context → Example → Evaluate. Name the task, give rich context, show an example of what "good" looks like, and evaluate the result critically. Your judgment stays in charge; AI supplies throughput.

🧪 Vision lab (do it now with your phone)

Take a photo of any document, receipt, whiteboard, or product around you. Upload it and prompt: “Extract everything useful from this image into a clean, structured format. If it's a table, give me a spreadsheet layout; if it's text, summarize the key points; if it's a product, describe it for a listing.”

Going deeper — choosing the right mode for the job

Multi-modal skill is not knowing that a tool can make images; it is knowing which mode removes the most friction for a specific task, and how each mode fails. Four questions decide it:

  • Where is the information right now? If it is on paper, a whiteboard or a screen, a photo is faster and more faithful than retyping. Vision models can extract tables and handwriting, but they misread low-contrast or skewed images, so always spot-check numbers against the source.
  • Does the output need to be exact or evocative? Image and video generators are evocative: excellent for mood, concept and draft visuals, weak at precise logos, exact product shapes, readable small text and correct hands. If exactness matters (a medical diagram, a contract, a real product), generate a draft and finish in a design tool or with a human designer.
  • Will a real person be represented? Generated people can drift into stereotype, and generated likenesses of real people raise consent issues. Commandment 3 applies: never generate a recognisable real person without consent, and review beneficiary images for dignity.
  • Is it audio for listening or for proof? Voice cloning can narrate your course in your voice — and can also impersonate you. Use cloning only on your own voice or with written consent, and label synthetic media where your audience would reasonably assume it is real.
Sector pattern. Across health, agriculture, education and retail the winning pattern is the same: capture (photo, voice note, scan) → structure (AI turns it into a table, summary or checklist) → human decision. A farmer photographs a diseased leaf; the AI suggests likely causes and questions to ask the extension officer — it does not prescribe the pesticide.

Provenance and disclosure

Major platforms increasingly attach content credentials (such as C2PA metadata) or watermarks to AI media, and many social platforms ask creators to label realistic synthetic content. Policies change often, so check the current rules of the platform you publish on. A simple house rule works everywhere: if a reasonable viewer would be misled about what is real, disclose.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a multi-modal workflow coach. My job is [describe]. List the five most time-consuming tasks in my week. For each, recommend the single best AI mode (vision, voice, image, video/audio, or text), the specific capture→structure→decide workflow, one failure mode to watch for, and how I would verify the output.

📚 Glossary

  • Multi-modal: AI that accepts or produces more than one format: text, image, audio, video
  • Content credentials (C2PA): Metadata standard recording how a piece of media was made or edited
  • Voice cloning: Synthesising speech that imitates a specific person's voice
  • Capture→structure→decide: Pattern: gather raw input, let AI organise it, keep the decision human

📖 References

  • Mollick, E. (2024). Co-Intelligence. Portfolio.
  • Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity — c2pa.org

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • The camera is a prompt. Most people never upload images — you'll leap ahead by treating your camera as an input device.
  • Voice for thinking, text for precision. Brainstorm by voice, then switch to text to refine the winner.
  • Task → Context → Example → Evaluate works in every mode and every industry.

📚 Glossary

  • Multi-modal: handling text, image, audio, and video together.
  • Vision input: giving the AI an image to analyze.
  • Voice mode: spoken, hands-free interaction.

📖 Explore further

  • Google AI Studio — aistudio.google.com — free multi-modal experimentation.
  • Your sector's specialization course goes deep on its specific use-cases.

quiz.q: A field officer needs 40 handwritten survey sheets turned into a spreadsheet by tomorrow. Which approach is MOST efficient while staying reliable?
opts: Ask an image generator to recreate the sheets cleanly before typing them manually
Dictate every sheet aloud into voice mode and ask the AI to type it up afterwards
Retype all sheets by hand, because AI cannot read handwriting at all
Photograph each sheet, have a vision model extract the table, then spot-check totals against the paper
quiz.x: Capture → structure → verify. Vision extraction is fastest; spot-checking guards against misreads.

quiz.q: A clinic wants an accurate anatomical diagram for patient leaflets. What is the soundest use of image generation here?
opts: Avoid AI entirely, because medical topics are banned on every image tool
Use it for a draft layout, then have the diagram checked and finished by a qualified person
Generate many versions and pick whichever one patients say they like best
Generate the final diagram directly, since modern models draw anatomy correctly
quiz.x: Generators are evocative, not exact. When accuracy matters, draft with AI and finish with expertise.

quiz.q: A marketer wants to clone a well-known local musician's voice for a radio ad, since 'everyone will recognise it'. What is the BEST response?
opts: Get the musician's written consent or use a different voice entirely
Proceed but lower the pitch slightly so it is not an exact match
Proceed if the ad is short and the station approves the script
Only use the clone if the ad is for a nonprofit cause
quiz.x: Cloning a real person without consent is impersonation — Commandment 3.

quiz.q: A trainer can either type notes during a 90-minute walk-and-think session or speak to voice mode. Why might voice mode produce BETTER raw material, not just faster?
opts: Voice models are trained on more data than text models
Voice mode cannot hallucinate because it repeats what you say
Speaking captures half-formed ideas the trainer would filter out while typing
Voice output is always more accurate than text output
quiz.x: Voice lowers the friction of capture, so more raw thinking survives to be structured later.

quiz.q: An NGO generates photos of 'rural beneficiaries' for a donor report. Several images show ragged clothing and despairing faces that do not match their community. What should happen?
opts: Keep them, since emotive images raise more money
Blur the faces so nobody can be identified
Regenerate or replace them; images must represent people with dignity and accuracy
Add a caption saying the images are illustrative and publish anyway
quiz.x: Stereotyped imagery harms the people represented. Dignity and accuracy are graded under Commandment 3.

quiz.q: Which task is the WEAKEST fit for current image generators without human finishing?
opts: A concept poster for an internal event
A product's exact registered logo on packaging artwork
Mood boards for a café redesign
Illustrations for a children's story draft
quiz.x: Exact brand marks need precision; generators often distort shapes and lettering.

quiz.q: A farmer photographs a diseased maize leaf and the AI names a likely fungus. What is the MOST responsible next step?
opts: Ignore the answer, because photos cannot show disease
Buy the fungicide the AI names, since it was confident
Post the AI's diagnosis to a farmers' group as confirmed
Use the AI's list of likely causes as questions for an extension officer or lab test
quiz.x: AI structures the problem; the decision rests on verified expertise.

quiz.q: A creator posts a realistic AI video of a 'street interview' that never happened, without any label. What is the core problem?
opts: Viewers would reasonably believe it was real, so it misleads without disclosure
AI video always has poor resolution
Video tools are not allowed to show streets
The video was probably too short to be useful
quiz.x: House rule: disclose when a reasonable viewer would be misled about what is real.

quiz.q: A teacher wants students to practise French conversation daily but has no time to supervise. Which mode fits BEST?
opts: Video generation, to make French clips
Image generation, to create French flashcards
Text summarisation of French news articles
Live voice conversation with the AI set to correct errors gently
quiz.x: Speaking practice needs a spoken partner; voice mode provides one on demand.

quiz.q: A vision model extracted a price table from a blurry photo. Totals look plausible. What is the BEST verification habit?
opts: Compare a sample of rows and the totals against the original before using it
Trust it, because plausible totals mean the extraction worked
Run the photo through a second AI and accept whichever is longer
Ask the same AI whether it made mistakes, and accept its answer
quiz.x: Plausible is not verified. Check against the source; self-assessment by the same model is weak evidence.

modules.t: Authoring With AI: Write Your First E-Book
modules.d: From blank page to published author — the Team21 process alumni have used to hit bestseller lists.
modules.body:
From reader to author in one week

Several Team21 alumni have published books — some reaching bestseller status — using the exact process in this module. It works because AI accelerates the mechanics (structuring, drafting, editing, formatting) while you provide the vision, the voice, and the lived truth that no model can invent. This is co-authoring, not outsourcing.

"Everybody has a book in them." The old obstacle was never ideas — it was the hundreds of hours of structuring and drafting. AI collapses that barrier. The vision still has to be yours; now the execution is finally within reach.

Step 0 — Decide before you draft

  • Topic & angle: what do you know, care about, or want to teach? What's your unique take?
  • Reader: who is this for, exactly? A specific reader beats "everyone."
  • Voice: which authors do you admire? Feed the AI two paragraphs of your own writing as a style anchor (few-shot, from Module 4).

The Team21 authoring pipeline

  1. Structure first. "You are a developmental editor. Help me outline a book on [topic] for [reader]. Propose 8–12 chapters, each with a one-line promise and 3–4 key points." Iterate until the skeleton excites you.
  2. Chapter by chapter. Draft one chapter at a time, feeding your outline + your voice sample. Never dump the whole book in one prompt — quality collapses.
  3. Your voice pass. Rewrite in your own words. The AI's draft is scaffolding; your edit is the building. This is where the book becomes yours — and where integrity lives.
  4. Developmental edit. "Act as a tough editor: where is this chapter weak, repetitive, or unclear? Rank the top five fixes." Then apply your judgment.
  5. Line edit & polish. Grammar, flow, transitions — AI is excellent here.
  6. Front & back matter: title options, subtitle, blurb, author bio, table of contents.
  7. Cover: generate concepts in Ideogram/Canva; a strong cover sells the book.
  8. Format & publish: export to the format your platform needs (e.g. Kindle Direct Publishing) and ship.
Integrity & honesty. Co-authoring with AI is legitimate and increasingly common — but be truthful. Don't claim solitary authorship where AI did heavy lifting, respect others' words (don't plagiarize), and verify every fact and quote the AI supplies (hallucinated citations are real). Commandments 2 and 3 apply to authorship.
🧪 Author's lab (copy → run to outline your book today)

You are an experienced developmental editor. I want to write a [type] book on [topic] for [specific reader]. Here are two paragraphs in my voice: [paste]. First, reflect back what you notice about my style in one line. Then propose a working title, a subtitle, and an outline of 8–12 chapters — each with a one-line promise to the reader and 3–4 key points. End by asking me which chapter I want to draft first.

🧪 Validated exercise

What should you feed the AI so it drafts in YOUR style (a Module-4 technique)? Two words:

Going deeper — protecting your voice, rights and reputation

The fastest way to ruin an AI-assisted book is to let the model's default voice replace yours. Default AI prose has recognisable tics: balanced triplets, "delve", "tapestry", tidy summaries at the end of every paragraph, and confident generalities with no lived detail. Readers notice. Three disciplines keep the book yours:

  • The 70/30 rule of thumb. Let AI carry structure, transitions and first drafts, but make sure the stories, examples, opinions and conclusions come from you. If a chapter contains no experience only you could have written, it is not finished.
  • The anecdote bank. Before drafting, record 20–30 voice notes of real stories, mistakes and turning points. Transcribe them and feed the relevant ones into each chapter prompt. This is your unfair advantage.
  • Fact and quote audit. AI invents statistics, studies and quotations with convincing citations. Every number and every quote in the manuscript must trace to a source you have opened yourself.

Rights, disclosure and publishing

Copyright rules for AI-assisted work are still evolving and differ by country. In the United States, the Copyright Office has said protection covers human authorship — your selection, arrangement and own writing — not material generated purely by AI. Self-publishing platforms such as Amazon KDP ask authors to disclose AI-generated content when publishing; check the current policy at the time you upload. Covers made with AI should avoid imitating a living artist's distinctive style or any trademarked character.

Editorial workflow that works: outline → chapter draft with anecdote → your rewrite → AI line-edit for clarity (not voice) → read aloud → beta readers → fact audit → format. Separate "make it clearer" from "make it sound better" — the second invites the AI to replace your voice.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a strict developmental editor. Here is a chapter draft: [paste]. 1) Highlight every sentence that sounds generic or AI-default. 2) Mark each claim or statistic that needs a source. 3) Point to where a personal story would make the chapter stronger, and ask me one question to draw that story out. Do not rewrite the chapter.

📚 Glossary

  • Style anchor: Samples of your own writing given to the AI to imitate
  • Anecdote bank: A collection of your real stories recorded before drafting
  • Line edit: Sentence-level editing for clarity and flow
  • Human authorship: The part of a work created by a person, which copyright can protect

📖 References

  • U.S. Copyright Office (2025). Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability.
  • Amazon KDP — Content Guidelines (AI-generated content disclosure).

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • One chapter per prompt. The single most common beginner mistake is asking for the whole book at once — output quality falls off a cliff.
  • Your edit is the moat. Anyone can generate a draft; your voice and truth are what make it worth reading and truly yours.
  • Ship the first one small. A tight 40-page guide published beats a 300-page masterpiece that never leaves your laptop.

📚 Glossary

  • Developmental edit: big-picture editing of structure and argument.
  • Line edit: sentence-level polish of grammar and flow.
  • Front/back matter: title page, TOC, blurb, author bio.
  • KDP: Kindle Direct Publishing, a common self-publishing platform.

📖 Explore further

  • Amazon KDP — kdp.amazon.com (self-publishing).
  • The Humanities specialization goes deeper on AI-assisted creative writing and authorship ethics.

quiz.q: An author's AI-drafted chapter is fluent but beta readers call it 'forgettable'. Which fix addresses the ROOT cause?
opts: Shorten the chapter so readers finish it faster
Ask the AI to use more vivid adjectives throughout
Add the author's own stories and opinions drawn from an anecdote bank
Switch to a newer model with better writing quality
quiz.x: Forgettable prose usually lacks lived detail. Only the author can supply it.

quiz.q: A draft cites 'a 2021 Harvard study showing 63% of readers prefer short chapters'. What should the author do FIRST?
opts: Keep it, since the citation looks specific and credible
Find and open the actual study before keeping the claim
Ask the AI to confirm the study exists and keep it if it says yes
Change the percentage to a round number to be safe
quiz.x: AI invents convincing citations. Only a source you opened yourself counts.

quiz.q: An author asks AI to 'make this chapter sound better' and the result no longer sounds like her. What prompt change would BEST prevent this?
opts: Ask the AI to rewrite it in a famous author's style
Ask for clarity edits only — fix confusion and errors, keep my wording and voice
Ask for a more formal tone
Ask for a shorter version with the same ideas
quiz.x: Separate clarity editing from style rewriting; 'sound better' invites voice replacement.

quiz.q: Why does the Team21 pipeline insist on drafting chapter by chapter rather than the whole book in one prompt?
opts: Platforms charge more for long prompts
AI cannot write more than 1,000 words at a time
Long single outputs lose quality, consistency and the author's control
quiz.x: Quality collapses on very long single generations; chapter-by-chapter keeps the author directing.

quiz.q: An author wants to publish a book that is almost entirely AI-generated with minimal edits, and register copyright in the US. What is the MOST accurate expectation?
opts: Protection likely limited to her own human contributions, such as selection, arrangement and writing
Protection depends only on the book's sales volume
Full protection, because she wrote the prompts
No book with any AI content can be published
quiz.x: US guidance protects human authorship, not purely AI-generated material.

quiz.q: A cover designer prompts 'in the exact style of [living illustrator]'. What is the BEST advice?
opts: Fine, because styles cannot be owned
Fine, if the illustrator's name is not on the cover
Fine, if the book is self-published
Describe the mood and elements you want instead of copying a living artist's signature style
quiz.x: Imitating a living artist's distinctive style raises ethical and reputational risk; describe the qualities instead.

quiz.q: Which pre-drafting activity gives an AI-assisted author the MOST distinctive raw material?
opts: Asking the AI to suggest popular topics
Writing a long list of chapter titles
Recording voice notes of real stories, mistakes and turning points
Reading three bestsellers in the genre
quiz.x: Your lived stories are the one input no model can generate.

quiz.q: An editor notices words like 'delve', 'tapestry' and a neat summary ending every paragraph. What does this MOST likely signal?
opts: Default AI phrasing has survived without a voice pass
The manuscript is ready for formatting
The author has an academic background
The book was translated from another language
quiz.x: These are common AI-default tics; they mean the author's rewrite step was skipped.

quiz.q: When uploading to a self-publishing platform, an author is unsure whether to declare AI use. What is the soundest approach?
opts: Never declare it, since readers cannot tell
Check the platform's current AI-content policy and disclose as it requires
Declare it only if the platform detects it
Remove all AI-assisted chapters before upload
quiz.x: Platforms such as KDP ask for disclosure; policies change, so check at upload time.

quiz.q: Which ordering of the final stages is MOST defensible?
opts: Fact audit → format → your rewrite → beta readers
Beta readers → format → read aloud → your rewrite
Format → beta readers → fact audit → read aloud
Read aloud → beta readers → fact audit → format
quiz.x: Polish and test content first, verify facts, then format the final text last.

modules.d: Your second graded build — run a full multi-modal media campaign for the organization you founded.
modules.body:
Your organization is real now — give it a voice

The nonprofit you founded in Lab 1 has stakeholders, and they want visibility. In this second graded plAIbox™ you become its one-person media team, producing a full multi-modal campaign in a week. This lab proves you can turn strategy into published assets — the exact skill that lets a single person run marketing that used to need a studio.

The mission set. Complete each mission using the recommended tools. Deliberately try several tools per task — comparing them IS the learning. Apply Task → Context → Example → Evaluate every time.

Mission 1 — Authentic program imagery

Generate images that authentically represent your beneficiaries and community with dignity (Ideogram, or the image tools in ChatGPT/Gemini/Grok). Evaluate for realism and respect — regenerate anything that feels stereotyped or demeaning. Commandment 3 is graded here.

Mission 2 — A launch poster with your slogan

Use Ideogram (best for crisp text-in-image) to produce a poster carrying your organization's name and tagline. Iterate on layout and color until it looks professionally designed.

Mission 3 — A 30-second promo video

Storyboard in your reasoning AI, generate clips (Runway/Veo), add a voiceover (ElevenLabs) and a music bed (Suno), and assemble in CapCut. Broadcast-style output from your laptop.

Mission 4 — A two-week social calendar

Draft platform-native posts for the channels your community uses (in your region, WhatsApp Broadcast + Facebook + TikTok). One idea → many formats. Include captions, hashtags, and best-time-to-post guidance.

Mission 5 — An audio spot for radio / WhatsApp

Write a 30-second script, generate a natural voiceover (ElevenLabs) in English and French, and a short Suno bed. Community radio and voice notes reach audiences that text never will.

Fei-Fei Li reminds us AI is made by people and lands on people. In media that means real audiences and real dignity — throughput without taste (or respect) is just noise. This lab grades both your output and your judgment.
🧪 Campaign lab (copy → run to storyboard Mission 3)

You are a creative director for a community organization. Our cause: [describe]. Storyboard a 30-second promotional video: 5–6 shots, each with a one-line visual description (for an AI video generator), a line of voiceover, and a mood for the music. Keep it emotionally honest and dignified — no stereotypes. Then give me the exact ElevenLabs voice direction and a Suno music prompt to match.

📝 Submission (graded by your mentor)

  • Program images (with a one-line dignity rationale), the poster, the promo video, the two-week calendar, and the bilingual audio spot.
  • A short tool-comparison note: which tool won each mission for you, and why.
  • Your prompt log with iterations — again, half the grade.

Going deeper — running a campaign like a producer

Media Week is graded on more than pretty assets. Professional producers work from a creative brief, keep a consistent brand system, and measure results. Use this structure before generating anything:

  • Brief: objective (one measurable outcome, e.g. 50 volunteer sign-ups), audience, key message, call to action, channels, deadline.
  • Brand kit: two or three colours with hex codes, one or two fonts, logo files, a tone-of-voice paragraph and a reusable style prompt. Paste the style prompt into every image request so assets look like one family.
  • Storyboard before video: six to eight shots, each with duration, visual, voiceover line and on-screen text. Generators make short clips; the story comes from your edit.
  • Accessibility: captions on every video (most social video is watched muted), alt text on images, readable contrast on posters.
Choosing between tools. Compare tools on the same brief and score them: fidelity to the prompt, text rendering, consistency across a set, cost, licence terms. Free tiers often restrict commercial use or add watermarks — read the terms before using assets for a real organisation.

Measuring the campaign

Decide your metrics before posting. Vanity metrics (likes, views) are easy to inflate; outcome metrics (sign-ups, donations, enquiries) tell you whether the campaign worked. Use a unique link or code per channel so you know which asset drove results, then ask AI to analyse the numbers and propose one change for week two.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a creative director. My organisation is [name, mission]. Write a one-page creative brief for a two-week campaign with one measurable objective, then a brand kit (colours with hex codes, font pairing, tone of voice) and a reusable image style prompt I can paste into every generation so assets stay consistent.

📚 Glossary

  • Creative brief: One-page plan stating objective, audience, message, channels and deadline
  • Brand kit: Colours, fonts, logo and tone rules that keep assets consistent
  • Storyboard: Shot-by-shot plan of a video before production
  • Outcome metric: A measure of the result you want, such as sign-ups, rather than attention

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Compare, don't commit. Run Mission 1 in two different image tools; you'll instantly see each one's strengths.
  • Repurpose ruthlessly: one promo video becomes shorts, stills, and a poster — maximum output per idea.
  • Check the rights tier: if you'll use audio/music commercially, confirm the plan grants a commercial license.

📚 Glossary

  • Platform-native: content shaped for a specific platform's format and norms.
  • Storyboard: a shot-by-shot plan for a video.
  • Bed (audio): background music under a voiceover.

📖 Explore further

  • The Sports, Media & Entertainment specialization builds this into a full production pipeline.
  • CapCut — capcut.com for assembly.

quiz.q: A team generated 30 beautiful images, but together they look like they come from different organisations. What would have prevented this?
opts: Generating images at a higher resolution
A brand kit with a reusable style prompt pasted into every request
quiz.x: Consistency comes from a shared style system, not from tool choice alone.

quiz.q: A promo video gets 12,000 views but zero volunteer sign-ups. What is the MOST useful conclusion?
opts: Views from AI videos are not counted properly
The campaign succeeded, because views measure reach
The video should be longer next time
Attention did not convert; review the call to action and the audience targeting
quiz.x: Views are a vanity metric; the objective was sign-ups.

quiz.q: Why storyboard a 30-second promo before generating any clips?
opts: It is required for copyright registration
Generators produce short shots; the story and pacing come from your planned edit
Video tools refuse prompts without a storyboard
quiz.x: Clips are raw material; the storyboard holds the narrative together.

quiz.q: An assistant wants to use a free-tier image tool's output on the NGO's printed banners. What should be checked FIRST?
opts: Whether the tool's free-tier terms permit commercial or organisational use
Whether the image looks professional enough
Whether competitors use the same tool
Whether the banner printer accepts PNG files
quiz.x: Licence terms and watermarks vary by tier; check before real-world use.

quiz.q: Most of the campaign's audience watches on mobile with sound off. Which production choice matters MOST?
opts: A professional music bed from Suno
Burned-in captions and clear on-screen text
quiz.x: Muted viewing means the message must be readable, not just audible.

quiz.q: Two channels drove traffic but the team cannot tell which produced the donations. What fix belongs in next week's plan?
opts: Ask donors in person where they saw the campaign
Post at the same time on every channel
Use a unique link or code for each channel
quiz.x: Per-channel tracking links show which asset actually drove outcomes.

quiz.q: Ideogram produced a poster with the slogan spelled correctly, while another tool garbled it. What does this comparison teach?
opts: Ideogram is better at every task
The other tool is broken and should be reported
Tools differ in strengths; compare them on the same brief
Text should never appear in posters
quiz.x: Comparing tools on identical briefs is the learning objective of Media Week.

quiz.q: A generated image of beneficiaries looks striking but shows a scene the community says is untrue to their lives. What is the graded response?
opts: Replace it, because accuracy and dignity are part of the grade
Add a small 'AI image' label and keep it
Keep it, since it attracts attention
Use it only on social media, not in reports
quiz.x: Commandment 3 is graded in Mission 1; striking does not excuse misrepresentation.

quiz.q: Which campaign objective is BEST written?
opts: Get 50 volunteer sign-ups via the campaign link in 14 days
Post every day for two weeks
quiz.x: A strong objective is specific, measurable and time-bound.

quiz.q: After week one, the AI analysis suggests five changes. What is the MOST disciplined approach for week two?
opts: Apply all five at once to maximise improvement
Apply the single highest-impact change so its effect can be measured
Apply none, because AI analysis is unreliable
quiz.x: Changing one variable at a time shows what actually works.

modules.t: Entrepreneurship With AI I: WHY, Problems & Finance
modules.d: Find your informed WHY, turn problems into businesses, and let AI run the numbers.
modules.body:
Every business begins with an informed WHY

Before tools and tactics comes purpose. The entrepreneurs who last are driven by a WHY strong enough to survive hard weeks — and informed enough to meet real demand. This module helps you find yours, convert a problem into a venture, and use AI as your first analyst and finance team. There are no shortcuts to durable income; purpose and diligence come first, and AI multiplies both.

Kai-Fu Lee calls this the "age of implementation": advantage has shifted from those who invent AI to those who apply it fastest to real problems. An entrepreneur with AI is a small team — this module is where you start acting like one.

Step 1 — Problems are your business

Every successful business is a solution to a problem people will pay to remove. Your first job is problem-hunting:

  • What frustrates you, your family, your community daily?
  • What do people around you complain about or waste money and time on?
  • Where do you see inefficiency you could fix?

Use AI to widen and sharpen the list: "You are a venture analyst. Based on these frustrations in [my community]: [list], identify the 5 with the strongest business potential. For each: who has the problem, how painful it is, what they pay today, and a one-line solution."

Step 2 — Find your informed WHY

Let AI interview you: "Ask me 5 questions, one at a time, to uncover my entrepreneurial WHY from my skills, passions, and the problems I care about. Then summarize my WHY in one powerful sentence and name the niche where it meets paying demand." A clear WHY is your compass and your marketing.

Step 3 — Validate before you build

  • Talk to 5 real potential customers (AI drafts your interview questions, never fakes the answers).
  • Check demand: "What signals would tell me people actually want this, cheaply, before I invest?"
  • Size it roughly: "Estimate the realistic local market for [idea] and the assumptions behind that estimate."

Step 4 — Let AI run the finance

  • Startup costs: "List every likely startup cost for [business] at small scale, with rough local figures I can adjust."
  • Pricing: "Propose three pricing tiers with the logic behind each."
  • Break-even: "At these costs and this price, how many sales do I need monthly to break even? Show the math."
  • Simple projection: a 12-month best/base/worst revenue sketch — you supply reality, AI supplies structure.
Field truth: AI will happily produce optimistic numbers. Your job (Commandment 2) is to challenge them: "What am I underestimating? What kills this business in year one?" The devil's-advocate prompt is worth more than the rosy plan.
🧪 WHY-finder lab (copy → run now)

You are a sharp, encouraging business coach. Ask me five questions, one at a time, to uncover my entrepreneurial WHY from my skills, passions, and the problems I see around me in [my city]. After my answers, summarize my WHY in one powerful sentence, name the single niche where it meets paying demand, and list three low-cost ways to validate that demand this week.

🧪 Validated exercise

Every successful business is fundamentally a solution to a ___.

Going deeper — validating before you build

AI makes it easy to produce a convincing business plan for a business no one wants. The antidote is evidence from real customers before investment. Three techniques from lean startup practice:

  • Problem interviews. Talk to 10–15 people who have the problem. Ask about the last time it happened, what they did, and what it cost them. Avoid pitching your idea — people are polite and will say they love it. Past behaviour beats future promises.
  • Smoke tests. Before building, offer the product: a simple landing page, a WhatsApp catalogue, a pre-order list. Measure how many people take a real step — leave a number, pay a deposit.
  • Riskiest assumption first. List every assumption (people will pay 2,000 FCFA; suppliers deliver weekly; delivery costs under 10%). Test the one that would kill the business if wrong.

Unit economics with AI as your finance assistant

Before forecasting revenue, understand one sale. Contribution margin = price − variable cost per unit. Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin. Example: a juice stand sells at 1,000 FCFA, ingredients and cup cost 400, so each sale contributes 600. With 180,000 FCFA monthly rent and wages, break-even is 300 juices a month, about 10 a day. Ask AI to build the sheet, but check every formula yourself and replace its assumptions with your own quotes from real suppliers.

Watch for AI optimism. Models default to round, hopeful numbers for market size and conversion. Ask: "Give me a pessimistic, realistic and optimistic case, and tell me which numbers you assumed."
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a sceptical investor. Here is my business idea and my assumptions: [paste]. List every assumption, rank them by how badly the business fails if each is wrong, and design a test I can run within 7 days and under 20,000 FCFA (or $40) for the top three. Then build a simple break-even calculation and show your formulas.

📚 Glossary

  • Smoke test: Offering a product before building it to measure real demand
  • Contribution margin: Price minus variable cost per unit
  • Break-even: The sales volume where total contribution covers fixed costs
  • Riskiest assumption: The belief that would sink the business if false

📖 References

  • Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown.
  • Fitzpatrick, R. (2013). The Mom Test.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Challenge every number. Ask "what would make this fail?" before "what would make this succeed?"
  • Validate cheaply first. A WhatsApp poll or a pre-order beats a business plan for proving demand.
  • Your WHY is marketing. The sentence AI helps you craft becomes your pitch, your bio, and your ads.

📚 Glossary

  • WHY: your informed core purpose — compass and marketing.
  • Validation: cheap evidence that people want your solution.
  • Break-even: the sales level where revenue covers costs.

📖 Explore further

  • The Entrepreneurship & Growth specialization scales this to a full operating model.

modules.t: Entrepreneurship With AI II: BMC + SOSTAC
modules.d: Your whole business on one page (Business Model Canvas) and a marketing plan that executes (SOSTAC).
modules.body:
Two frameworks that turn an idea into a running business

Module 11 found your WHY and validated the problem. Now you design the machine. Two battle-tested frameworks do the heavy lifting — and AI fills each block in minutes instead of weeks.

The Business Model Canvas — your business on one page

Created by Alexander Osterwalder and used by millions of entrepreneurs and Fortune 500 teams, the BMC's nine blocks answer three questions: Who do we serve? What value do we deliver? How do we make money?

  • 1. Customer Segments — who exactly are your best customers?
  • 2. Value Proposition — why do they choose YOU over alternatives?
  • 3. Channels — how do you reach and deliver to them?
  • 4. Customer Relationships — how do you win, keep, and grow them?
  • 5. Revenue Streams — how exactly does money come in?
  • 6. Key Resources — what assets do you need?
  • 7. Key Activities — what must you do well?
  • 8. Key Partnerships — who helps you deliver?
  • 9. Cost Structure — what does it cost to run?

AI prompt: "You are a startup strategist. Draft a Business Model Canvas for [my validated idea]. Fill all nine blocks with specific, realistic content for my context: [describe]. Then flag the two riskiest assumptions I should test first."

SOSTAC® — the marketing plan that actually executes

Developed by PR Smith, SOSTAC is six stages that take you from analysis to action and control:

  • Situation — where are we now? (market, competitors, your position)
  • Objectives — where do we want to be? (specific, measurable goals)
  • Strategy — how do we get there? (the big approach)
  • Tactics — the details of strategy (channels, content, offers)
  • Action — who does what, when? (the execution plan)
  • Control — how do we measure and adjust? (KPIs, review cadence)
A plan you can hold in your head beats a binder no one reads. BMC fits on one page; SOSTAC fits on two. AI drafts both in an afternoon — then you spend your energy on the two riskiest assumptions, where it actually matters.
Regional marketing reality (2025 data for our home market): WhatsApp reaches ~95% of smartphone users with strong conversion; Facebook (~6M+ users locally) delivers high geo-targeted ROI; TikTok (~4M) can drive outsized campaign returns; Instagram peaks evenings; LinkedIn (~1.5M) is your B2B engine. Weight your SOSTAC Tactics toward where your customers actually are — the full data lives in the Entrepreneurship specialization.
